performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: Hartmann designs a clock shaped like a hut on chicken legs; Mussorgsky sends its witch flying through the air in a mortar. Baba Yaga’s furious ride runs straight into The Great Gate of Kyiv.

sections.label: A · The witch’s hammering ride
sections.mNote: Feroce: hard accents and repeated Gs drive the opening

sections.label: B · Flute above a creeping bass
sections.mNote: Andante mosso: rocking thirds surround the low tune

sections.label: A′ · The hammering G returns
sections.mNote: Allegro molto restores the witch’s two-beat stride

sections.label: Coda · Rising octaves towards the gate
sections.mNote: Continuous semiquavers climb into the finale without a break

cues.title: The witch stamps twice
cues.text: F♯ and low G collide, with a whole bar of silence after them. Soon the Gs keep hammering. The marking is feroce — ferocious — and Ravel sends a trumpet theme through the racket, answered by other brass.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 1–56; trumpet and brass scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and a creeping bass
cues.text: In the Andante mosso, a flute flits above the slower line of bassoon and double bass. The score begins this middle passage with G and E rocking back and forth. Harp, celesta and strings gather around the low tune.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, Andante mosso, bars 95 onward; instruments: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clock on chicken legs
cues.text: Hartmann’s sketch is a design for a metal clock: a little hut on chicken legs, decorated with cocks’ heads. Mussorgsky adds the owner. Baba Yaga flies about in a mortar, hunting for victims.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg describes the clock and Baba Yaga’s mortar: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition. Peter Laki identifies the surviving sketch: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky

cues.title: The witch rides again
cues.text: Allegro molto: the hammering Gs return in two-beat bars. The trumpet’s strident tune and answering brass are back. The quiet middle has left the witch with plenty of energy for another chase.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 123 onward; orchestral return: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Up towards the gate
cues.text: The closing semiquavers run through octave after octave and climb to G. There is no pause at the top: attacca sends that G straight into the E♭ major opening of The Great Gate of Kyiv.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, Baba Yaga bars 187–211 and the first bar of The Great Gate: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/baba-allegro-molto.ily
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Hammered G becomes a rocking third
transitions.to: B · Flute above a creeping bass
transitions.how: The hard repeated Gs shrink into a quiet figure rocking between G and E. Andante mosso slows the pulse. Ravel brings flute, bassoon and double bass forward, with harp and celesta around them; the heavy brass retreat.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 89–103: repeated G, Andante mosso and rocking G–E figure. Scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: G breaks out of the tremolo
transitions.from: B · Flute above a creeping bass
transitions.how: B, D♯ and G tremble under a fermata at the end of the middle. A forceful G starts Allegro molto, back in two-beat bars. The repeated-note figure rebuilds the witch’s stride, and the brass tune follows.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 122–145: final tremolo, fermata and G-led Allegro molto; the orchestral return is described by Joanna Wyld.

transitions.title: The octaves climb into E♭ major
transitions.to: Coda · Rising octaves towards the gate
transitions.how: The short phrases become a continuous stream of semiquavers in octaves. After sweeping down, they climb to G, the third of the E♭ major chord that opens the finale. The last bar is marked attacca: the gate appears before the witch’s flight can stop.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 187–211 and the opening of The Great Gate; Mutopia transcription. Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note also describes the uninterrupted join.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who can no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate: close-fitting uniform, polished manners, well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later another hospital would provide his most familiar likeness: Repin’s painting of a man in a dressing gown, hair in disorder, eyes still alert. There is a great deal of music between those two rooms.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano; his nurse’s stories stirred the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he went to school in Saint Petersburg and studied piano with Anton Gerke. The School of Guards Cadets followed in 1852, then a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid to publish his first piano piece, a polka. The boy could play for a drawing room before he knew how an orchestra worked.
